Located approximately 100 miles (161 km) northeast of Fairbanks, this 27-mile (44 km) hiking trail traverses a series of alpine ridge tops entirely above timberline. The trail was built for hikers, but is open to all forms of non-motorized use. The Pinnell Mountain Trail is marked with rock cairns as it crosses open tundra with views north to the Yukon River and south to the Alaska Range. Wooden posts along the trail show the mileage from the start at Eagle Summit to the trail's end at Twelvemile Summit. Two shelters provide refuge from storms, but hikers should come prepared for unpredictable, dramatic alpine weather. The Act states that plain writing means "writing that is clear, concise, well-organized, and follows other best practices appropriate to the subject or field and intended audience." The Census Bureau has long sought to improve communications with the public, dependent as we are on public cooperation in our censuses and surveys. We at the Census Bureau are committed to writing new documents in plain language. Search Twitter YouTube Facebook Instagram Flickr LinkedIn Canyons of the Ancients National Monument | Colorado View Map In Full Screen Canyons of the Ancients National Monument, located in the Four Corners region of southwestern Colorado, protects a stunning cultural landscape with the highest known density of archaeological sites in the United States. Encompassing 176,000 acres of public lands, the Monument features more than 8,300 documented sites—including villages, kivas, field houses, cliff dwellings, petroglyphs, and ancient roadways—with estimates suggesting over 30,000 yet to be recorded. These sites offer a window into over 12,000 years of human history, primarily shaped by Ancestral Puebloan cultures and their descendants. The area continues to be a living landscape used today for traditional purposes, recreation, hunting, livestock grazing, and energy development. It also encompasses Cross Canyon , Sego Lily, and Cahone Canyon Wilderness Study Areas. pages.text: Plant extinctions are shaking Earth’s green foundation | National Geographic Gardeners’ demand for the Chilean crocus nearly drove it extinct in the wild by the 1950s. But in 2001, a thriving population was found on land south of Santiago Photograph By SELECTPHOTO/ALAMY STOCK PHOTO ENVIRONMENT VANISHING Plant extinctions are shaking Earth’s green foundation Compared with birds, mammals, and amphibians, more plants have vanished in the wild since 1900. What’s the cost to ecosystems? By Michael Greshko 3 min read This story appears in the October 2019 issue of National Geographic magazine. When you conjure up “extinction” in your mind’s eye, you probably see an animal—a dodo , perhaps, or a Tasmanian tiger . But the biodiversity crisis isn’t just faunal, it’s floral too. Since the 1750s, at least 571 species of plants have gone extinct in the wild, according to a global survey recently published in Nature Ecology & Evolution . More than eight plant species have disappeared every three years, on average, since 1900. pages.description: It isn't as far-fetched as it sounds.
pages.text: Polar Bears in the Roman Colosseum? | National Geographic By Candida Moss Published September 28, 2026 Want to make sure you get every Stones & Bones newsletter? Put your email here . There’s a strange and intriguing reference in the writings of a first-century Roman poet who describes a showdown between bears and seals (or, as he called them, “sea-calves”) in the Colosseum. Only polar bears are known to fight seals, so this raises a question no modern scholar has yet been able to answer: How on Earth would arctic bears have traveled to the heart of the Roman Empire? A clue to the ursine mystery has recently emerged—in the first English language book on Scandinavian Roman-era history, Dagfinn Skre's The Northern Routes to Kingshi p . Skre places Sweden, Norway, and Denmark at the periphery of the empire, showing that Denmark was only a four-week march from the Roman frontier. And in fact, the Roman military was recruiting from the region by the late first century A.D. So the social networks and infrastructure were in place to facilitate the movement of exotic animals that Rome craved for its spectacles. I reached out to Michael Kulikowski, a professor of classics at Penn State who wrote about Skre’s work for the London Review of Books , for more on how polar bears could have ended up on the sands of Rome’s most famous arena. Polio Vaccination July 9, 2024 Español Key points There is no cure for polio (or poliomyelitis), but it can be prevented with safe and effective vaccination. CDC recommends that children get 4 doses of polio vaccine to protect them against severe polio disease, including paralysis. Most adults in the United States were vaccinated as children and are therefore likely to be protected from getting polio. Introduction The best way to protect against polio , or poliomyelitis, is to get vaccinated. Polio vaccination has been part of the routine childhood immunization schedule in the United States for decades. It's still part of the routine childhood immunization schedule. Inactivated polio vaccine (IPV) is the only polio vaccine that has been given in the United States since 2000. Oral polio vaccine (OPV) is used in other countries. Available vaccines There are two types of vaccines that protect against polio. Inactivated polio vaccine (IPV) The only polio vaccine that has been used in the United States since 2000. pages.title: Pompeii's Secrets: How AI is Rewriting the Story of Mount Vesuvius | National Geographic
pages.description: It was one of history’s most dramatic moments—but the eruption of Mount Vesuvius wasn’t a single disaster. Recent evidence reveals how three settlements faced three distinct fates, reshaping our understanding of how ancient Romans lived and died.
pages.text: Pompeii's Secrets: How AI is Rewriting the Story of Mount Vesuvius | National Geographic By Sam Kean Photographs by Paolo Verzone Video by Massimo Nicolaci Published July 23, 2026 Outside, the world was vanishing. A scum of ash was thickening on the surface of the Gulf of Naples, and black fumes were swallowing the sky above. In a waterfront warehouse in the Roman town of Oplontis, five dozen people cowered in terror. Some clutched gold coins and jewelry—family wealth snatched up in panic. Others gripped common iron tools and little more. One young woman hugged her swollen belly, terrified for the unborn child inside. Their ages and social classes varied widely, but they’d likely all gathered in a storeroom on the water’s edge for the same reason: to await a rescue boat they were increasingly fearful would never come. In A.D. 79, Mount Vesuvius blew its top, raining ash over the Campania region of Italy, near modern-day Naples, and burying surrounding communities beneath as much as 60 feet of volcanic debris. What happened that day in A.D. 79 began with a single event, the eruption of Mount Vesuvius . But each settlement in the volcano’s shadow—including the most famous, Pompeii —experienced a distinct catastrophe depending on its location relative to the volcano and the timing, speed, and direction of the material Vesuvius spewed. A handful of lucky folks within those communities escaped. The Executive Order 13496: Notification of Employee Rights Under Federal Labor Laws Poster – Contractors may reproduce the poster but may only use exact duplicates. The poster must be 11 by 17 inches. pages.text: Premier League incident-by-incident: Was it a bad weekend for VAR? - BBC Sport Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Manchester United's last-gasp equaliser against Aston Villa survived a VAR review for a potential foul By Dale Johnson Football issues correspondent Published 9 November 2026 Whisper it quietly, but the statistics say video assistant referee decisions have been pretty good in the Premier League so far this season. The Key Match Incidents (KMI) Panel, which looks at every contentious decision and votes whether it is right or wrong, reported just two VAR errors after eight rounds of matches. At the same stage last season, there had been six mistakes. Then came this weekend, during which almost every top-flight game had a controversial decision. BBC Sport looks at most of these situations - there really were too many to do them all - and assesses the likelihood that the KMI Panel will add to the list of errors. Manchester United 4-4 Aston Villa Incident 1: Penalty awarded to Manchester United for a foul by Boubacar Kamara on Matheus Cunha in the 16th minute. Verdict: The spot-kick was awarded because the Villa defender went through Cunha to win the ball. Replays clearly showed the first contact was on the Brazilian's foot. What the KMI Panel might say: This will be a correct decision. Incident 2: Possible foul by Senne Lammens on Aston Villa goalkeeper Zion Suzuki before Patrick Dorgu's 96th-minute equaliser. Verdict : There are similarities to a goal Arsenal scored at Old Trafford last season, when William Saliba leant into United goalkeeper Altay Bayındır.
